meta.ogDescription: An old anonymous saying, not Patton's. The earliest close match is a 1905 filler item. Quote Investigator calls the Patton connection weak.

answer.label: Not George S. Patton — an old anonymous saying
answer.authorDates: Earliest close match 1905 · unsigned filler item in The Westminster, Philadelphia
answer.sourceLine: No speech, letter or book of Patton’s is known to contain this line. Quote Investigator ↗ found the earliest close match in an anonymous 1905 filler item: “When everybody thinks alike, nobody will think at all.” QI ties the Patton credit to a 1979 memoir by Porter B. Williamson and calls the connection “weak.” In QI’s chronology, the “somebody isn’t thinking” wording first appears in a 1990 quotation compilation.

“The connection to George Patton is weak.”

source.excerpt: It was not necessary for staff officers to agree with Gen. Patton. He followed Ben Franklin’s idea of no one was thinking if everyone was thinking alike.
trail: 1905: The earliest close match Quote Investigator found ↗ is an unsigned filler in The Westminster: “When everybody thinks alike, nobody will think at all.” QI notes 19th-century precursors as well.
1915: Walter Lippmann writes “Where all think alike, no one thinks very much” in The Stakes of Diplomacy ↗. It is a real early variant, but it is not the popular wording.
1919 and 1922: Stanford professor Edward Krehbiel uses the saying in two speeches. The second time he hedges it with “as has been said” (Barry Popik ↗).

1979 onward: Williamson’s memoir ties the idea to Patton. A 1990 compilation prints “If everyone is thinking alike then somebody isn’t thinking” under his name. Wikiquote now lists the line only among unsourced Patton quotes ↗.
source.excerptNote: From Porter B. Williamson’s I Remember General Patton’s Principles (1979), as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. Williamson, writing from memory, describes it as a Franklin idea that Patton followed. He does not quote Patton saying it, and his wording (“no one is thinking”) is not the popular one.

source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording has no identifiable author or originating work. It is a late rephrasing of an anonymous saying that appeared in print by 1905, so quotle.info asserts no copyright status for it. The 1979 Williamson memoir and the 1990 compilation that carry Patton-credited versions are themselves modern works and are not public domain.

author.name: George S. Patton
author.heading: About George S. Patton
author.metaLine: 1885–1945 · U.S. Army general, World War II
author.bio: George Smith Patton Jr. was a U.S. Army general who commanded the Seventh Army in the Mediterranean and then the Third Army in France and Germany after the Normandy invasion. His blunt, profane style makes him a magnet for tough-sounding management maxims. This one appears in none of his known writings. It reached him through a subordinate’s 1979 memoir, which framed it as Ben Franklin’s idea that Patton followed.

copyAttribution: “If everyone is thinking alike, then somebody isn't thinking.” This anonymous saying is often misattributed to George S. Patton. Its earliest close match is an unsigned 1905 filler item: “When everybody thinks alike, nobody will think at all.” (Quote Investigator)

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: This saying has drifted through dozens of wordings and many famous names. Quote Investigator ↗ records these attributions:

items.why: The credit traces to Porter B. Williamson’s 1979 memoir. According to QI ↗, Williamson was relying on memories of events decades earlier and called the line a principle Patton followed, not something Patton said. In How Google Works (2014), Eric Schmidt and Jonathan Rosenberg used the popular wording and added in a footnote that they could find no direct proof Patton said it.
Williamson wrote that Patton “followed Ben Franklin’s idea,” and a 1995 Utah column later credited Franklin outright. QI ↗ cites no Franklin source for the saying.
Lippmann did write “Where all think alike, no one thinks very much” in The Stakes of Diplomacy (1915) ↗. Later rephrasings were credited to him as well, but the anonymous 1905 filler is older.
The Stanford professor closed a 1919 speech with “When everybody thinks alike nobody thinks at all.” In 1922 he introduced it with “as has been said” (Barry Popik ↗).

A 1964 Dallas newspaper credited Kennedy with “If everyone is thinking alike, then no one is thinking at all.” In 1988 Charlotte Mayor Sue Myrick was quoted saying “If everybody’s thinking alike we’re not thinking” (QI ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The saying is anonymous. Its earliest close match is a 1905 filler item, and the Patton version is a later rephrasing that, in QI’s words, has only a “weak” connection to him (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why Patton got it
lead: Williamson served with Patton in World War II. His 1979 book I Remember General Patton’s Principles listed “If everyone is thinking alike, no one is thinking” among Patton’s decision-making principles on its back cover. The book called the idea Franklin’s, but it put a famous general’s name next to an old saying. By 1990 a compilation printed the now-familiar “somebody isn’t thinking” form under Patton’s name (Quote Investigator ↗).

The attribution spread from there. When Google executives Eric Schmidt and Jonathan Rosenberg quoted the line in How Google Works (2014), they admitted in a footnote that they could find no proof of it in Patton’s memoir War As I Knew It or in his famous speech to the Third Army.
context.pull: “But the Internet says he did, so it must be true (that’s a joke).” — Schmidt & Rosenberg, How Google Works, footnote
